opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think reasoning is in a really interesting place, because it's the newest of the big scaling axes, and that means we're still early on the curve.

With pre-training, we've spent years scaling compute, data, and model size, and the gains are now harder to get. Each step up costs a lot more. Reasoning, meaning training models with reinforcement learning to think longer before they answer, is much earlier in that process. There's a lot of low-hanging fruit left. So I'd expect rapid progress over the next year or two, with much better capability from relatively modest increases in compute.

As the technique matures, I think a few things change.

First, the domains will broaden. Early on, reasoning worked best where you could clearly check the answer: math, competitive programming, problems with a right answer. The hard part is extending it to fuzzier domains where it's harder to say whether the model did well, like writing a strategy memo, doing research, or handling a long, messy task in a real codebase. Figuring out how to give good reward signals there is where much of the work goes.

Second, the time horizon grows. Today's reasoning is mostly thinking for seconds or minutes on one problem. The natural next step is models that work coherently for hours, keeping track of what they've tried, recovering from mistakes, and using tools along the way. That's really what turns reasoning into agents. It's less "answer this hard question" and more "go do this job."

Third, efficiency becomes important. Right now these models often think much longer than they need to. As the field matures, a lot of effort will go into getting the same quality with less thinking, and into knowing when to think hard and when to just answer. That matters a lot for cost and latency, and so for which products are viable.

The big picture is that we haven't hit a wall. We've moved from one scaling curve that was flattening to a new one that's still steep. Eventually reasoning will mature and get expensive at the margin too, like pre-training did. But we're not there yet, and I think the next couple of years will bring big jumps in what these systems can reliably do.

r001.rationale: It says reasoning is early on its scaling curve, with “a lot of low-hanging fruit left,” allowing rapid progress from modest compute increases.

r002.rationale: It mentions models using tools as their time horizons grow, but does not distinguish how obvious tool use is conceptually from how difficult it is to implement.

r003.rationale: It says reasoning will eventually mature and become more expensive at the margin, but does not clearly predict slower progress as readily available improvements are exhausted.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest in plain prose.

Well, I think the big thing to understand about reasoning is that it's really the third major paradigm we've found, after pre-training and then the post-training that made things like ChatGPT work. And what's interesting about it is that it gives you a new axis to scale along. With pre-training, you scale the data and the compute that goes into the model up front. With reasoning, you're scaling the compute the model spends at test time, when it's actually thinking about your problem. And the early results on that curve looked a lot like the early pre-training results, which is to say the improvements were very fast and very steep, because you're starting from a point where nobody had really tried it before.

So the way I'd expect it to mature is that you see the same pattern we saw with pre-training. The low-hanging fruit gets picked, and then progress becomes more about engineering and systems and scale, rather than one clever idea unlocking everything. That doesn't mean it slows to nothing. It means the gains come from doing a lot of things well, from better environments, better reward signals, letting the model think for longer and use tools while it thinks, and from putting the reasoning model into a larger system, like an agent, where it can take actions over hours instead of seconds.

And honestly, I think that's where the most important change happens. Right now, when people think of reasoning, they picture a model solving a hard math problem in one sitting. But as the technique matures, reasoning becomes the thing that lets a model carry out long tasks reliably, check its own work, recover from mistakes. That's the capability that turns these models from very good question answerers into things that can actually do work for you. So the headline benchmarks will keep improving, but the practical shift is that the length and complexity of the tasks you can hand off keeps going up. And I think that trend, more than any single benchmark, is what people should pay attention to.

r001.rationale: The response says early gains were fast because reasoning had barely been explored, then describes the low-hanging fruit being picked.

r002.rationale: It mentions using tools while reasoning, but does not distinguish the idea’s conceptual obviousness from the difficulty of implementing it.

r003.rationale: It predicts that after the low-hanging fruit is picked, progress shifts from steep gains to slower, cumulative engineering and systems work.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re moving toward systems that can spend more time working through a problem before answering. That gives us another way to improve performance: you can train a better model, but you can also give that model more time to reason when the problem warrants it.

The interesting question is how effectively it uses that time. Can it notice that an approach isn’t working, back up, and try something else? Can it check its answer? As those capabilities mature, I’d expect progress to show up less as a model giving an impressive answer to a single question and more as a model reliably completing a difficult task over many steps.

That reliability is a big deal. Getting something right occasionally is exciting, but getting it right consistently is what makes it useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses giving a model more time to reason, but does not say a new technique benefits from a backlog of readily available improvements.

r002.rationale: It mentions noticing a failed approach and trying another, but does not discuss tool use or distinguish its conceptual simplicity from implementation difficulty.

r003.rationale: The response predicts continued progress in reliability, not that progress will slow as readily available improvements are exhausted.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re moving from a world where progress comes mostly from training bigger models to one where we can also get better answers by giving a model more time to work on a problem. That creates a new dimension for improvement: how effectively can it use that time to explore different approaches, check its work, and recover from mistakes?

As the technique matures, I’d expect that process to become more efficient. You don’t want a model to spend a minute thinking about something it could answer immediately. You want it to recognize the hard problems and devote effort where that effort actually helps. And the test is whether it can reliably solve increasingly difficult problems, not just produce a longer explanation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using more time to explore and check work, but does not say the technique benefits initially from a backlog of readily available improvements.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss adding tool use during reasoning or distinguish how obvious that idea is from the difficulty of implementing it.

r003.rationale: It predicts greater efficiency and solving harder problems, but does not predict progress slowing as readily available improvements are exhausted.
